tool.name: npm
tool.tagline: The package manager and registry client that ships with Node.js
tool.description: npm is the package manager bundled with Node.js and the client for the npm registry, the largest package registry in the world. It installs and locks dependency trees, runs project scripts, manages monorepo workspaces and publishes packages, so mastering it means reproducible builds, safer dependencies and smooth releases.

glossary.def: An option added after a command to change what it does, such as -D or --save-dev after npm install. Many flags have a long and a short spelling.
A rule in package.json saying which versions of a package are acceptable, such as ^1.4.2 (any 1.x at or above 1.4.2) or >=1.2.0 <1.5.0.
A version published for testing before the real one, named with a suffix such as 2.0.0-beta.3. It sorts before 2.0.0 and ordinary ranges skip it.
A named label a package's maintainers attach to one version, such as latest, next or beta. npm install pkg installs the version that latest points to.
A package your project needs only because one of your packages needs it. You never listed it, but it is installed and locked all the same.
To save a set of changes into version control as one named step in the project's history. A committed file is shared with the whole team.
What happens when two people change the same part of a file and version control cannot combine the two versions; someone must choose or fix by hand.
A package.json script with a special name, such as prepare, postinstall or prepublishOnly, that npm runs by itself at a fixed moment of installing or publishing.
A package your package plugs into but does not ship itself, such as React for a React component library. The project that installs you must provide it.
The single packed-up file (.tgz) that holds a package. npm uploads one when you publish and downloads one when someone installs.
The @name/ prefix in a package name like @acme/ui. Every package under one scope belongs to one organization or user, and a scope can be sent to its own registry.
A package's written list of what changed in each version, where breaking changes are announced.
Logging in with a password plus a second proof, usually a code from your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough.
One of several packages kept in subfolders of one repository and managed together by the root package.json, with one install and one lock file.
A published notice that a specific range of versions of a package has a known security problem, with its severity and the version that fixes it.
A key inside a package's exports map, such as import, require or types, that picks which file to load depending on how the package is being used.
The problem when a package ships both an ES module and a CommonJS build and a program loads both: two copies with separate state that disagree with each other.
All the packages and tools your project depends on, and the people and systems that publish them. A supply-chain attack slips harmful code into one of them.
Publishing from a registered CI workflow that proves its identity with a short-lived token from the CI provider, so no long-lived npm token has to be stored.
A signed record, attached to a published package, of which repository, commit and CI workflow built it, kept in a public log so it cannot be quietly changed.
The part of npm that plans and carries out installs: it reads the current node_modules and the lock file, works out the tree that should exist, and changes the disk to match.
npm's habit of placing each installed package as high in node_modules as possible, usually at the top level, so several packages can share one copy.
A package your code imports without declaring it, which only works because another dependency pulled it in and npm placed it at the top of node_modules.
Publishing a harmful package under a name that is one typo away from a popular one, such as expresss, and waiting for people to mistype.
An attack that publishes a public package with the same name as a company's private one, hoping installs pick the public copy instead.

concepts.name: The npm CLI and the registry
concepts.summary: Find your way around the npm command: inspect packages with view, see what is installed with ls, and get help for any command.
concepts.why: Knowing a dozen commands well saves hours of guessing about what is installed and why.
concepts.body:
You already use `npm install` and `npm run`. The name npm covers two things: the **registry** — the website at `registry.npmjs.org` that stores millions of published packages — and the `npm` program you type commands into, which ships with Node.js and talks to it. Node 24 comes with npm 11. npm 12 (July 2026) needs Node 22.22 or 24.15 and later and is stricter about a few things; these lessons point them out as they come up.

Beyond install and run, these commands answer most everyday questions:

- `npm view <pkg>`: asks the registry about a package without installing it: its versions, dependencies, publish dates, where its code is developed, and its **dist-tags** (named labels such as `latest` that point at one version; the next lesson covers them). `npm view react versions --json` lists every version.
- `npm ls <pkg>`: where a package sits among your installed packages; `npm ls --all` prints the whole tree.
- `npm explain <pkg>` (or `npm why`): the chain of packages that caused it to be installed.
- `npm outdated`: which of your dependencies have newer versions.
- `npm exec <name>` / `npx <name>`: run a package's command-line tool. npm looks for it in `node_modules/.bin`; if it isn't installed, npm downloads it to a temporary place first.
- `npm pkg get|set|delete`: read or change one setting in package.json from the terminal, without editing the JSON by hand.
- `npm doctor` checks your setup, `npm config list` shows your settings, and `npm help <command>` opens the manual page.

The options you add after a command, like `--save-dev`, are called **flags**. Most have a long and a short spelling: `--save-dev` is `-D`, `--global` is `-g`. npm 12 is stricter here: a misspelled or shortened flag is an error instead of a warning, so spell flags out in scripts.

A global install (`-g`) puts a tool's command on your **PATH** — the list of folders your terminal searches when you type a command name — so it works from any folder. But the project doesn't know about it. For project tools, prefer `devDependencies` plus `npx`.
concepts.code:
npm --version                  # 11.x with Node 24
npm view express version       # latest published version, e.g. 5.1.0
npm view express dist-tags     # { latest: '5.1.0', next: '...', ... }
npm view express time.modified # last publish date

npm ls express                 # where it is installed in this project
npm explain debug              # why is "debug" in my project?
# debug@4.4.0
# node_modules/debug
#   debug@"^4.4.0" from express@5.1.0
#   node_modules/express
#     express@"^5.1.0" from the root project

npm outdated                   # Current / Wanted / Latest per dependency
npm pkg get scripts.test       # read one setting from package.json
npx eslint --version           # run the project's copy, or a temporary download
takeaways: `npm view` asks the registry about a package without installing it
`npm ls` and `npm explain` answer what is installed, and why
`npx` / `npm exec` run a package's command-line tool
npm 12 rejects unknown or shortened flags
pitfalls: Installing project tools globally, so the project only works on one machine.

quiz.q: Which command shows the chain of packages that pulled a dependency into your tree?
quiz.explain: `npm explain` (alias `npm why`) prints the dependents that require a package.

concepts.name: Version ranges and dist-tags
concepts.summary: Read every version range npm accepts, install prereleases from dist-tags like next, and decide when to pin exact versions.
concepts.why: Ranges decide which code you actually run after the next install.
concepts.body:
From the Node lessons you know `^1.4.2` (minor and patch updates allowed) and `~1.4.2` (patch updates only). npm understands several more ways to write a **version range** — a rule saying which versions of a package are acceptable:

- `1.x` or just `1`: any version that starts with 1. `*`: any version at all.
- Comparisons: `>=1.2.0 <1.5.0`. Put a space between conditions when both must hold, or `||` when either is fine: `^2.0.0 || ^3.0.0`.
- `1.2.3 - 1.4`: everything from 1.2.3 up to, but not including, 1.5.0.

A **prerelease** is a version published for testing before the real one, with a suffix like `2.0.0-beta.3`. It sorts before `2.0.0`, and a range only matches prereleases if the range itself names a prerelease of that same `major.minor.patch`. So `^1.0.0` never installs `2.0.0-beta.1`, even though that is newer than any 1.x.

A **dist-tag** is a named label a package's maintainers attach to one version. `latest` is what `npm install pkg` gives you. Maintainers publish betas under another tag, usually `next` or `beta`, so they don't become `latest`. Install one with `npm install react@next`; see a package's tags with `npm view react dist-tags`.

**Pinning** means writing an exact version like `1.4.2` instead of a range. `npm install -E pkg` (`--save-exact`) does it for one package; `npm config set save-exact true` makes it the default. Your lock file already fixes what is installed, so pinning in package.json mainly matters for tools whose updates you want to choose one by one.

If you publish a library, keep ranges (usually `^`): when two libraries need the same package, a range lets the project share one copy instead of installing two.
concepts.code:
# The semver package has a small command-line tool:
# which of the versions listed fit the range?
npx semver -r "^1.4.2" 1.4.1 1.9.0 2.0.0           # 1.9.0
npx semver -r "1.2.3 - 1.4" 1.2.3 1.4.9 1.5.0      # 1.2.3, 1.4.9
npx semver -r "^2.0.0 || ^3.0.0" 2.5.0 3.1.0 4.0.0  # 2.5.0, 3.1.0
npx semver -r "^1.0.0" 2.0.0-beta.1                # (nothing: prerelease excluded)

npm view vite dist-tags          # { latest: '8.x.y', beta: '...', ... }
npm install vite@beta            # install whatever "beta" points to
npm install -E typescript@5.9.3  # writes "typescript": "5.9.3"
npm install 'lodash@>=4.17.21 <5'
takeaways: Ranges: `^`, `~`, `1.x`, comparisons, `||` and `a - b`
Prereleases only match ranges that name a prerelease
Dist-tags (`latest`, `next`, `beta`) are movable labels
`-E` pins an exact version; libraries should keep ranges
pitfalls: Expecting `^1.0.0` to pick up `2.0.0-rc.1`; prereleases of other versions never match.

quiz.explain: The right-hand side 1.4 means every 1.4.x, so the range ends just before 1.5.0 and 1.4.9 fits.

concepts.name: package-lock.json and npm ci
concepts.summary: Understand what the lock file records, when npm install changes it, how npm ci uses it, and how to fix a lock file merge conflict.
concepts.why: The lock file is what makes 'works on my machine' work on every machine.
concepts.body:
`package-lock.json` records the exact set of packages npm installed: for each one its version, the address it was downloaded from (`resolved`) and a hash of its contents (`integrity`). npm works it out from your package.json ranges plus whatever the registry held at install time.

When it changes:

- `npm install` with no arguments keeps every locked version that still fits package.json, and only picks versions for what is new or no longer fits.
- `npm install pkg`, `npm update` and `npm uninstall` change it on purpose.
- `npm ci` never changes it. It deletes `node_modules`, installs exactly what the lock file says, and **fails** if package.json and the lock file disagree. Use it wherever installs must be repeatable: on a build server, and when building the copy that goes live.

Most teams have a build server that installs the project and runs its tests on every change; that automation is called **CI** (continuous integration). `npm ci` is the install command for it.

Your packages have packages of their own. Those are your **transitive dependencies**: you never listed them, but they are installed all the same, and the lock file pins them too. Never delete the lock file to "fix" an install: you silently upgrade hundreds of them at once.

Save (**commit**) the lock file to version control, for apps and libraries alike. A library's lock file never affects the people who install it: npm ignores lock files inside dependencies.

Sometimes two people change the lock file at the same time and version control can't combine the two versions: a **merge conflict**. Fix package.json first, then run `npm install`; npm can repair a lock file that still contains the conflict marks. Commit the result.

For the copy that goes live, `npm ci --omit=dev` (or setting `NODE_ENV=production`) skips devDependencies. And a note on npm 12: it dropped `npm shrinkwrap`, an older kind of lock file. An `npm-shrinkwrap.json` is no longer read, so rename it to `package-lock.json` if you still have one.
concepts.code:
# Developer: add a dependency (updates package.json AND the lock file)
npm install zod
git add package.json package-lock.json

# Build server: exact, clean, repeatable
npm ci                     # fails if package.json and the lock file disagree
npm ci --omit=dev          # live install without devDependencies

# Merge conflict in package-lock.json:
git checkout --theirs package-lock.json   # or fix package.json conflicts first
npm install                               # npm rebuilds a consistent lock file
git add package-lock.json
takeaways: The lock file pins every version, download address and integrity hash
`npm ci` installs exactly the lock file and never changes it
Commit it; never delete it to fix problems
Fix a lock file merge conflict by re-running `npm install`
pitfalls: Running `npm install` instead of `npm ci` on the build server, so it may install something other than the reviewed lock file.

quiz.q: What does `npm ci` do if package.json asks for a range the lock file does not satisfy?
quiz.explain: `npm ci` refuses to proceed when the two files are out of sync.

concepts.name: npm scripts and lifecycle hooks
concepts.summary: Write package.json scripts, pass arguments with --, use pre/post hooks and npm_ environment variables, and run installed tools with npm exec.
concepts.why: Scripts are the shared, written-down list of commands every JavaScript project is run with.
concepts.body:
The `scripts` section of package.json maps a name to a command, exactly what you would type in a terminal. `npm run <name>` runs it, with `node_modules/.bin` added to the front of PATH, so tools installed in the project run without a global install. `npm test`, `npm start`, `npm stop` and `npm restart` work without `run`. `npm run` on its own lists every script.

Details worth knowing:

- **Arguments**: everything after `--` is passed on to the script: `npm run test -- --watch`.
- **Pre and post hooks**: if a script named `prebuild` exists it runs before `build`, and `postbuild` runs after, automatically.
- **Environment**: a running script can read environment variables such as `npm_package_name`, `npm_package_version` and `npm_lifecycle_event` (the name of the script being run).

Some script names npm runs on its own, during other commands. These **lifecycle scripts** include `prepare` (after `npm install` in your own project, and before publishing), `prepublishOnly` (just before publishing), and `preinstall`, `install` and `postinstall` (when your package is installed as a dependency of someone else's project).

npm hands each command to the computer's **shell** — the program that reads a typed command and runs it: `sh` on macOS and Linux, `cmd.exe` on Windows. If teammates use different systems, stick to what both shells understand, or set the `script-shell` setting.

Node 22 and later also offer `node --run <script>`, which starts faster but skips pre/post hooks and npm's environment variables.

Keep scripts short. Put anything complicated in a file under `scripts/` and run it with `node`.
takeaways: `npm run` adds node_modules/.bin to PATH, so project tools just work
Pass arguments to a script after `--`
pre<name> and post<name> hooks run automatically
`node --run` is faster but skips hooks
pitfalls: Using commands only Bash understands in scripts that Windows teammates must run.

quiz.q: What runs when you type `npm test` and `pretest` is defined?
quiz.explain: npm runs the pre hook first, then the script, then any post hook.

concepts.name: Dependency types: dev, peer, optional
concepts.summary: Choose between dependencies, devDependencies, peerDependencies and optionalDependencies, and install only some of them with --omit.
concepts.why: The wrong dependency type bloats the live install or breaks your library's users.
concepts.body:
package.json can list packages under several headings, and npm treats each one differently.

`dependencies`: packages your code needs when it runs. They are installed for your project, and for anyone who installs your package.

`devDependencies`: tools needed only while developing — TypeScript, linters, test tools, bundlers. Installed for your project, never for people who install your published package. Leave them out of the live copy with `npm ci --omit=dev`.

`peerDependencies` are for packages that plug into another package. A library of components for React (a popular library for building web pages) doesn't ship its own React. It declares `"react": "^18 || ^19"` as a **peer dependency**: "the project that installs me must provide React, and one of these versions". That way the project has one React, not two. Since npm 7, a missing peer is installed automatically, and peer ranges that can't all be satisfied fail with `ERESOLVE`. A peer that isn't strictly needed is marked optional in `peerDependenciesMeta`.

`optionalDependencies`: installed if possible. If one fails to install — typically a package built for one operating system only — the install still succeeds, so your code must cope with it missing.

`bundleDependencies`: copied inside your package's **tarball** — the single packed-up file npm uploads when you publish and downloads when someone installs — instead of being fetched separately.

For an app that runs in the browser, which a bundler packs up before shipping, the line between dependencies and devDependencies matters less, because the bundler decides what reaches the browser. Many teams still keep tools used only for building under devDependencies, so installs on the build server stay fast.

`--legacy-peer-deps` makes npm ignore peer dependencies entirely, and `--force` makes it accept conflicts. Both hide real incompatibilities; prefer fixing versions, or the `overrides` setting (an Advanced lesson).
takeaways: dependencies ship to users of your package; devDependencies never do
peerDependencies: the project that installs you provides it (React, add-ons)
optionalDependencies may fail to install; your code must cope
Avoid `--legacy-peer-deps` and `--force` as permanent fixes
pitfalls: Listing react as a regular dependency in a component library, so projects end up with two copies of React.

quiz.q: An add-on package for the build tool Vite must share the installing project's own copy of `vite`. Where should `vite` go?
quiz.explain: Add-ons plug into the project's own copy, so vite is a peer; it is also a devDependency so the add-on can be tested locally.

concepts.name: Updating dependencies safely
concepts.summary: Keep dependencies current with outdated, update and deliberate major upgrades, remove duplicate versions, and let bots do the routine work.
concepts.why: Stale dependencies accumulate vulnerabilities and painful multi-major upgrades.
concepts.body:
A healthy routine:

- `npm outdated` shows **Current** (installed), **Wanted** (newest within your range) and **Latest** (the `latest` dist-tag). Lines in red are behind what your range already allows.
- `npm update` moves everything to **Wanted** and updates the lock file. Fairly safe: it stays within the same major for `^` ranges.
- Major upgrades are explicit: `npm install pkg@latest`, then read the package's list of changes (its **changelog**) and run the tests. Upgrade big frameworks one major at a time.
- `npm dedupe` simplifies the tree by moving shared packages up so fewer duplicate versions are installed; `npm find-dupes` shows what it would do.
- `npm install --before=2026-09-01`, or the `min-release-age` setting (a number of days), only picks versions published before a date. That helps reproduce an old install, and avoids brand-new releases that might turn out to be compromised.

Automate it. **Renovate** and **Dependabot** are bots that open **pull requests** — proposed changes that teammates review before they are merged — for each update, group related packages, and can merge patch updates automatically once CI passes. Keep the lock file in those pull requests so CI tests exactly what will ship.

Transitive dependencies update through their parents' ranges. If a vulnerable transitive package is held back by a parent you cannot upgrade, use `overrides` (Advanced lesson).
concepts.code:
npm outdated
# Package     Current  Wanted  Latest  Location
# express       5.0.1   5.1.0   5.1.0  node_modules/express
# typescript    5.8.3   5.9.3   5.9.3  node_modules/typescript
# vitest        3.2.4   3.2.4   4.0.8  node_modules/vitest

npm update                     # express -> 5.1.0, typescript -> 5.9.3
npm install vitest@latest      # deliberate major upgrade, then run tests
npm test

npm find-dupes                 # what npm dedupe would change
npm dedupe

# Only accept versions that have been public for at least 3 days
npm config set min-release-age 3 --location=project
takeaways: outdated: Current vs Wanted (in range) vs Latest
`npm update` stays within ranges; majors need `pkg@latest`
`npm dedupe` removes duplicate versions
Bots (Renovate, Dependabot) keep updates small and continuous
pitfalls: Letting dependencies rot for two years, then facing five breaking majors at once.

quiz.q: `npm outdated` shows Wanted 5.9.3 and Latest 6.0.0 with range `^5.8.0`. What does `npm update` install?
quiz.explain: `npm update` moves to the newest version that satisfies the declared range.

concepts.name: .npmrc, scopes and private registries
concepts.summary: Configure npm per project, user and machine with .npmrc, send scoped packages to a private registry, and pass access tokens safely.
concepts.why: Companies install from private registries, and the build server needs to log in without the secret leaking into the code.
concepts.body:
npm reads its settings from several places, highest priority first: command-line flags, environment variables named `npm_config_<key>`, the **project** `.npmrc` (next to package.json), the **user** `~/.npmrc`, the global `$PREFIX/etc/npmrc`, and built-in defaults. `npm config list` shows the merged result and where each value came from.

A **package scope** is the `@name/` prefix in package names like `@acme/ui`; every package under one scope belongs to one organization or user. You can send a whole scope to a different registry:

```ini
@acme:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com
```

Everything else still comes from the default `registry`.

A private registry needs to know who is asking. `npm login --registry=...` proves it once and saves an **access token** — a secret string you send with each request to show you are allowed in — in the user `.npmrc`, never the project one.

A committed project `.npmrc` must never contain a real token. Instead write a reference to an environment variable, which npm fills in when it runs: `//npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}`. The build server then provides `NPM_TOKEN` as a secret.

Other useful project settings: `engine-strict=true` (refuse Node versions outside `engines`), `save-exact=true`, `min-release-age`, and `audit-level`.

Companies often run their own registry server (Verdaccio, Artifactory, Nexus, GitHub Packages, AWS CodeArtifact) that keeps a copy of public packages and holds the private ones. npm 12 reports an error for unknown `.npmrc` keys, so a typo no longer passes silently.
concepts.code:
# .npmrc in the project root (committed: no secrets, only references)
@acme:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com
//npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=${NODE_AUTH_TOKEN}
engine-strict=true
save-exact=true
min-release-age=3

# Inspect the settings in force and where they come from
npm config list
npm config get registry                 # https://registry.npmjs.org/
npm config get @acme:registry           # https://npm.pkg.github.com

# Build server: provide the token as a secret environment variable
NODE_AUTH_TOKEN=$GITHUB_TOKEN npm ci
takeaways: Settings layer: flags > environment > project > user > global > defaults
Send a scope to another registry with `@scope:registry=`
Write `${ENV_VAR}` in .npmrc instead of a real token
npm 12 rejects unknown settings
pitfalls: Committing a .npmrc that contains a real `_authToken` value.

quiz.q: How should a committed project .npmrc provide a registry token?
quiz.explain: npm expands environment variables in .npmrc, so the secret stays in CI settings.

concepts.name: Publishing a package
concepts.summary: Prepare a package with files and the required details, preview it with npm pack, bump versions with npm version, and publish with dist-tags.
concepts.why: Shipping a library or an internal package means uploading a clean tarball with exactly the files you meant.
concepts.body:
Before publishing, decide **what goes in the tarball**. Use the `files` list in package.json (e.g. `["dist"]`) to say which files to include, rather than listing what to leave out in `.npmignore`; package.json, README and LICENSE are always included. Preview with `npm pack --dry-run`, which lists every file and its size. Leaked `.env` files and test data are common mistakes.

Required details: a unique `name` (scoped names like `@you/pkg` can't clash with anyone else's), a `version`, and ideally `description`, `license`, `repository` (where the source lives) and `engines`, plus the package's **entry points** — the files that importing it actually loads (a later lesson).

Versioning: `npm version patch|minor|major` bumps `version`, then commits and tags the change in Git (`v1.2.4`), running the `preversion`, `version` and `postversion` scripts. `npm version prerelease --preid=beta` makes a beta.

Publishing:

- `npm publish` uploads to the registry and moves the `latest` dist-tag. A scoped package is private by default; pass `--access public` the first time you publish an open-source one.
- Publish prereleases with `--tag next` so they do not become `latest`.
- `prepublishOnly` is the place to run the build and the tests.
- Accounts must use **two-factor authentication** (2FA): a code from your phone as well as the password. Automated releases should use **trusted publishing** from the build server rather than long-lived tokens (a later lesson).

Mistakes: `npm deprecate pkg@1.2.3 "reason"` warns users off a version. `npm unpublish` is only freely allowed within 72 hours (and when nothing depends on the version) and is discouraged. A version number can never be reused.
concepts.code:
# package.json (excerpt):
#   "name": "@ann/slugify", "version": "1.0.0",
#   "files": ["dist"], "license": "MIT",
#   "scripts": { "build": "tsc", "prepublishOnly": "npm run build && npm test" }

npm pack --dry-run
# npm notice package: @ann/slugify@1.0.0
# npm notice 1.1kB LICENSE
# npm notice 642B  README.md
# npm notice 2.3kB dist/index.js
# npm notice 812B  package.json
# npm notice total files: 4

npm version minor               # 1.0.0 -> 1.1.0, git commit + tag v1.1.0
npm publish --access public     # first publish of a public scoped package
git push --follow-tags

npm version prerelease --preid=beta   # 1.1.1-beta.0
npm publish --tag next                # latest stays at 1.1.0
takeaways: Use `files` and check `npm pack --dry-run` before publishing
`npm version` bumps, commits and tags
Publish prereleases under a dist-tag other than latest
Versions can never be reused; deprecate instead of unpublishing
pitfalls: Publishing a beta without `--tag`, making it the version everyone installs.

options: Without it, the beta becomes the `latest` dist-tag
quiz.explain: npm moves `latest` on every publish unless you choose another tag.

concepts.name: Workspaces and monorepos
concepts.summary: Manage several packages in one repository with npm workspaces: one install, one lock file, linked local packages and per-workspace commands.
concepts.why: Apps that share code with their own libraries usually keep everything in one repository, and workspaces are npm's built-in support for that.
concepts.body:
A **monorepo** is one repository that holds several packages: an app, the libraries it shares with other apps, and so on. npm supports it with **workspaces**: one root package.json lists the folders that hold the member packages:

```json
{ "name": "acme", "private": true, "workspaces": ["packages/*", "apps/*"] }
```

Running `npm install` at the root installs every workspace's dependencies into one root `node_modules` and writes **one lock file**. Each workspace is also placed in that `node_modules` as a **symbolic link** — a special file that makes the folder appear there without copying it. So `apps/web` can `import "@acme/ui"` and get the local source, without publishing anything.

Working with them:

- Target one workspace with `-w`: `npm install zod -w apps/api`, `npm run build -w @acme/ui`.
- Run in all of them: `npm run test --workspaces --if-present` (`-ws` for short); `--if-present` skips packages that have no such script.
- Add one workspace as a dependency of another by name: `npm install @acme/ui -w apps/web`; npm links the local copy when the version matches.
- `npm ls -w apps/web` shows one workspace's tree.

Limits: npm runs workspace scripts one after another, with no notion of which packages depend on which, no caching of results, and no "only what changed". Larger monorepos add **Turborepo** or **Nx** on top for that, or use **pnpm** workspaces, whose strict layout stops a package from importing something it never declared.

Mark the root `"private": true` so it can never be published by accident.
concepts.code:
# Layout:  package.json (root)  packages/ui/package.json  apps/web/package.json
cat package.json
# { "name": "acme", "private": true,
#   "workspaces": ["packages/*", "apps/*"],
#   "scripts": { "test": "npm run test --workspaces --if-present" } }

npm install                          # one install, one package-lock.json
ls -l node_modules/@acme/            # ui -> ../../packages/ui (symlink)

npm install @acme/ui -w apps/web     # local package as a dependency
npm install -D vitest -w packages/ui # dev dependency of one workspace
npm run build -w @acme/ui            # run one workspace's script
npm run test -ws --if-present        # run everywhere it exists
npm ls -w apps/web --depth=0
takeaways: Root `workspaces` patterns list the member packages
One install, one lock file, local packages linked in
`-w <name>` targets one workspace, `-ws` all of them
Add Turborepo or Nx for ordering and caching
pitfalls: Forgetting `"private": true` on the root and publishing the whole monorepo by accident.

quiz.q: How does `apps/web` get the local `@acme/ui` code without publishing it?
options: npm copies the source on every build
npm places a symbolic link to the workspace in node_modules
quiz.explain: Workspaces are linked into the root node_modules with symbolic links, so the import finds the local folder.

concepts.name: Auditing and overriding dependencies
concepts.summary: Read npm audit reports, fix vulnerabilities with audit fix or targeted upgrades, and force transitive versions with `overrides`.
concepts.why: Most vulnerabilities live in transitive dependencies you never chose directly.
concepts.body:
`npm audit` sends the list of installed packages to the registry's database of known security problems (**advisories**) and lists every match with its severity, the vulnerable versions and the chain of packages that pulled it in. `npm install` prints a short summary automatically.

Fixing, in order of preference:

- `npm audit fix`: upgrades within your declared ranges. Safe to run.
- Upgrade the direct dependency that pulls in the vulnerable package (use `npm explain <pkg>` to find it).
- `npm audit fix --force` may install **breaking** major versions. Review its plan; never run it blindly in CI.
- **overrides**: in the root package.json, force a version anywhere in the tree, or only under one parent:

```json
"overrides": { "semver": "^7.5.4", "jest": { "micromatch": "^4.0.8" } }
```

Overrides only work in the root project (not in published packages). Use `$name` to point at your own direct dependency's version and keep the two in step. Remove an override once the package's maintainers ship a fix.

Judgement matters: an advisory in a build-only tool that never sees data from outside is lower risk than one in the code that reads incoming requests. Use `npm audit --omit=dev` to focus on what ships, and `--audit-level=high` in CI to fail only above a threshold.

`npm audit signatures` checks the registry's signatures and the provenance records (next lesson) of your installed packages.
concepts.code:
npm audit
# semver  <7.5.2
# Severity: moderate
# semver vulnerable to Regular Expression Denial of Service
# fix available via `npm audit fix`
# node_modules/old-lib/node_modules/semver
#   old-lib  *  Depends on vulnerable versions of semver

npm audit fix                       # in-range upgrades only
npm explain semver                  # who depends on it?
npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high   # CI gate on shipped code

# package.json: force a patched version for all or one subtree
#   "overrides": {
#     "semver": "^7.6.0",
#     "old-lib": { "semver": "^7.6.0" }
#   }
npm install && npm ls semver        # verify every copy is patched
npm audit signatures                # check registry signatures and provenance
takeaways: `npm audit fix` stays in range; `--force` can break things
Upgrade the direct parent first, overrides as a last resort
Overrides only work in the root package.json
Gate CI on shipped code with `--omit=dev --audit-level`
pitfalls: Running `npm audit fix --force` in CI and shipping surprise major upgrades.

quiz.q: A vulnerable transitive package is pinned by an unmaintained parent. Which tool forces a patched version?
quiz.explain: Overrides replace a package's version anywhere in the tree from the root project.

concepts.name: Package entry points: exports and types
concepts.summary: Define what a package lets others import with the exports field, with separate entries for ESM, CommonJS and types, and private imports.
concepts.why: The exports map controls what users of your package can import, and mistakes break bundlers, Node and TypeScript in different ways.
concepts.body:
The `exports` field in package.json lists a package's **entry points**: the files that importing the package, or a path inside it, actually loads. Once `exports` is present, users can import **only** the listed paths; a deep import like `pkg/dist/internal.js` fails with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`. Because nothing else is reachable, you can reorganise the rest freely.

```json
"exports": {
  ".": { "types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "import": "./dist/index.js", "require": "./dist/index.cjs" },
  "./utils": "./dist/utils.js",
  "./package.json": "./package.json"
}
```

The keys inside an entry are **conditions**, and the first one that fits wins, in the order written: `types` (TypeScript), `import`, `require`, `node`, `browser`, `development`/`production`, and `default` as the fallback. Put `types` first and `default` last.

Related fields:

- `main` and `module` are the older entry-point fields; keep `main` only for old tools.
- `type: "module"` makes `.js` files ES modules; `.cjs` and `.mjs` decide per file.
- `imports` defines private shortcuts starting with `#`, like `"#db": "./src/db/index.js"`, usable only inside the package.
- `sideEffects: false` tells bundlers that unused modules can be dropped entirely.

A package that ships both ESM and CommonJS risks the **dual package hazard**: both copies get loaded, each with its own variables, and they disagree. Since Node 22 can `require()` an ES module, publishing ESM only is increasingly practical. Check your package with `publint` and `@arethetypeswrong/cli`.
takeaways: `exports` lists the only importable paths
Conditions match in order: types first, default last
`imports` gives private `#` shortcuts inside the package
Check packages with publint and arethetypeswrong
pitfalls: Putting `types` after `import` in a condition object, so TypeScript never sees it.

quiz.q: A package has an `exports` map without `./dist/*`. What happens on `import 'pkg/dist/a.js'`?
quiz.explain: With `exports`, only the declared subpaths are accessible.

concepts.name: Trusted publishing and provenance
concepts.summary: Publish from CI with trusted publishing instead of long-lived tokens, and attach provenance so users can check where a package was built.
concepts.why: Stolen publish tokens are behind many attacks that slip harmful code into popular packages.
concepts.body:
All the packages your project depends on, and the people and systems that publish them, form its **supply chain**. A supply-chain attack slips harmful code into one link of it. Classic release automation was a weak link: it published with a long-lived token kept as a CI secret, and whoever stole the token could publish malware under your name. The registry now offers better options.

**Trusted publishing** replaces the stored token with a trust relationship. On npmjs.com, or with `npm trust github ...` (npm 11.15+), you register which CI workflow (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD and others) may publish the package. When that workflow runs `npm publish`, the CI provider hands it a short-lived identity token, and npm swaps that for permission to publish. The identity token follows **OpenID Connect** (OIDC), a standard way for one service to prove to another who is calling. There is nothing to store, rotate or leak. In GitHub Actions the job needs `permissions: id-token: write`.

**Provenance** is a signed statement, created automatically when you publish this way (or with `npm publish --provenance` when a token is still used), that records which repository, commit and workflow built the tarball. It is also written to a public, append-only record run by the Sigstore project, so it can't be quietly altered. The npm website shows a provenance badge; users check it with `npm audit signatures`.

**Staged publishing** (`npm stage publish`) lets CI upload a version that stays unavailable until a maintainer approves it with two-factor authentication, putting a human check back into automated releases.

Also: require two-factor authentication for publishing in the package settings, prefer narrowly scoped tokens with short expiry where a token is unavoidable, and keep the list of maintainers short.
concepts.code:
# .github/workflows/release.yml
name: release
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write          # lets npm obtain GitHub's identity token
jobs:
  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
          registry-url: https://registry.npmjs.org
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm publish --access public   # no NPM_TOKEN: trusted publishing + provenance
takeaways: Trusted publishing swaps a CI identity token for publish rights: no stored secret
Provenance links a tarball to its repository, commit and workflow
Staged publishing adds a human approval to automated releases
Users check provenance with `npm audit signatures`
pitfalls: Keeping a long-lived automation token in CI secrets after moving to trusted publishing.

quiz.q: What does a package's provenance let its users verify?
options: That the code has no bugs
Which repository, commit and CI workflow built the package
quiz.explain: Provenance is a signed statement about where and how the package was built.

concepts.name: How npm builds node_modules
concepts.summary: Understand npm's ideal tree, hoisting and duplication, phantom dependencies, install strategies, and how pnpm differs.
concepts.why: Most mysterious install bugs come from how the tree is laid out on disk.
concepts.body:
npm's installer is a component called **Arborist**. It works in phases: load the **actual tree** (what is in `node_modules`) and the lock file, compute an **ideal tree** that satisfies every range, then **reify** it: compare the two and add, remove or move packages on disk until they match.

Node finds `require("x")` by looking for a `node_modules/x` folder next to the requiring file, then in each parent folder upward. npm exploits that with **package hoisting** (the default `install-strategy=hoisted`): each package is placed as high as possible, ideally at the root, so every package can share it. When two packages need incompatible versions, one copy is hoisted and the other is nested under the package that needs it: `node_modules/a/node_modules/lodash`.

Consequences:

- **Phantom dependencies**: your code can import a hoisted package you never declared. It works until some parent stops depending on it. Add a lint rule for undeclared imports.
- **Duplicates**: several versions of one package can coexist; `npm ls pkg` and `npm dedupe` reveal and reduce them. Two copies of a package meant to exist once per program (React, a GraphQL library) cause "multiple instances" errors.
- The layout depends on install order and history, which the lock file pins.

Other strategies: `nested` (no hoisting), `shallow` (only direct dependencies at the top), and `linked`, which stores packages in `node_modules/.store` and places symbolic links to them, much like **pnpm**. pnpm keeps one copy of each package version on the whole machine, named by its content hash, and links into it; that saves disk space and makes phantom dependencies impossible. Yarn PnP drops `node_modules` entirely.
concepts.code:
mkdir layout-demo && cd layout-demo && npm init -y >/dev/null
npm install express@5 --silent
npm ls debug --all
# layout-demo@1.0.0
# └─┬ express@5.3.0
#   ├─┬ body-parser@2.3.0
#   │ └── debug@4.4.3 deduped
#   ├── debug@4.4.3
#   ...
ls node_modules | wc -l        # ~65 packages hoisted to the top level
node -e "require('debug')"     # works: a phantom dependency!

npm install --install-strategy=linked --silent
ls -A node_modules             # only express (+ .store, .package-lock.json)
node -e "require('debug')"     # Error: Cannot find module 'debug'
takeaways: Arborist: actual tree + lock file -> ideal tree -> reify
Package hoisting shares packages but enables phantom dependencies
Conflicting versions are nested under the package that needs them
The `linked` strategy and pnpm give strict, linked layouts
pitfalls: Importing a package that only exists because another dependency pulled it in.

quiz.q: Why can code `require()` a package not listed in its package.json under the default npm layout?
options: npm adds it to package.json automatically
It was hoisted to the root node_modules by another dependency
quiz.explain: Hoisting makes transitive dependencies visible at the top level, where Node's lookup finds them.

concepts.name: Inside package-lock.json
concepts.summary: Read lockfileVersion 3: the packages map keyed by install path, resolved URLs, integrity hashes, flags, and the hidden lockfile.
concepts.why: Reading the lock file directly answers questions no command does, and lets you review dependency changes in pull requests.
concepts.body:
Modern npm writes **lockfileVersion 3**. Its core is a `packages` object keyed by **install location**:

- `""` is the root project, repeating its dependency ranges.
- `"node_modules/express"` is a hoisted package; `"node_modules/a/node_modules/lodash"` a nested one. Workspaces appear by folder (`"packages/ui"`) plus a `link: true` entry under `node_modules`.

Each entry records:

- `version` and `resolved`: the exact tarball address. For private registries this reveals where packages come from.
- `integrity`: a hash of the tarball, normally `sha512-...`. npm checks every download against it, so a tampered registry or mirror is detected.
- The `dependencies`, `peerDependencies` and `optionalDependencies` ranges that package declares, plus `engines`, `os`, `cpu`, `bin` and `license`.
- Marks: `dev: true`, `optional: true`, `devOptional: true`, `peer: true`, `hasInstallScript: true` (a quick way to list the packages that run install scripts).

npm also keeps a **hidden lock file** at `node_modules/.package-lock.json`, a record of the actual tree that speeds up later installs.

The example is shortened. Reviewing lock file changes in pull requests is real security work: an unexpected `resolved` host, a git address, or a newly added package with `hasInstallScript` deserves a closer look. Tools like `lockfile-lint` automate the host and address checks.
takeaways: `packages` is keyed by install path; the root is ""
`integrity` hashes are checked on every download
Marks like dev, optional and hasInstallScript say what kind of entry it is
Review lock file changes: hosts, git addresses, install scripts
pitfalls: Approving pull requests without looking at lock file changes, where a malicious download address can hide.

quiz.q: What does npm do with the `integrity` field?
options: Uses it as a cache key only
Verifies the downloaded tarball's hash against it
quiz.explain: A mismatch means the tarball differs from what was locked, and the install fails.

concepts.name: Defending against supply-chain attacks
concepts.summary: Control install scripts with allowScripts, restrict git and URL dependencies, delay fresh releases, and harden CI installs.
concepts.why: Malicious package versions and install scripts are the most common way attackers reach developer machines and CI.
concepts.body:
Real attacks on the npm ecosystem take a few forms. **Typosquatting**: publishing `expresss` and waiting for typos. **Compromised maintainer accounts** publishing malicious versions of popular packages. **Dependency confusion**: publishing a public package with the same name as your private one, hoping the registry lookup picks it. And **install scripts** that steal tokens the moment you run `npm install`.

Defences built into npm:

- **Install script policy.** The `allowScripts` field in package.json lists which dependencies may run `preinstall`, `install` and `postinstall`. Manage it with `npm approve-scripts` and `npm deny-scripts`. In npm 11 it only reports unreviewed scripts; **npm 12 blocks unreviewed dependency install scripts by default**. `--ignore-scripts` turns them off entirely.
- **Git and address dependencies**: `allow-git` and `allow-remote` limit packages fetched from a git repository or a plain download address; npm 12 sets both to `none` by default.
- **Cooling-off period**: `min-release-age=3` (days) skips versions published minutes ago, the window in which most malicious releases are caught and removed.
- **Scoped private packages** sent to your own registry prevent dependency confusion.
- `npm ci` with a reviewed lock file, `npm audit signatures`, and provenance checks.

Around npm: run CI installs with no secrets in the environment, give the publish job its own minimal permissions, use trusted publishing, and consider services that screen packages (Socket, Snyk, GitHub dependency review) and flag suspicious new versions.
takeaways: Attacks: typosquats, hijacked maintainers, dependency confusion, install scripts
`allowScripts` plus approve-scripts/deny-scripts control install scripts (enforced in npm 12)
Restrict git and address dependencies, and wait out fresh releases with min-release-age
Keep secrets out of CI install steps
pitfalls: Running `npm install` in a CI job that also holds the credentials used to ship the app.

quiz.q: Why does a `min-release-age` of a few days reduce risk?
options: Most malicious releases are detected and removed within that window
quiz.explain: Compromised versions are usually caught quickly, so not installing brand-new releases avoids them.
